steps.say: Finding the side of a square from its area is taking a square root: \(\sqrt{9} = 3\), \(\sqrt{25} = 5\). When the area is not a perfect square, like 50, hunt for the biggest square hiding inside it: \(50 = 25 \times 2\), so \(\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25} \times \sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}\). Pulling out that square factor is simplifying a surd, the first move in this lesson.

steps: Simplify a surd by pulling out the largest square factor
Rationalise: multiply by the surd, or by the conjugate for a two-term denominator
Bounds: half a unit above and below the rounded value
Largest value of a/b: use upper a and lower b
method_card.title: Indices, Surds & Bounds
method_card.content:
Surds are exact square roots such as \(\sqrt{2}\). Simplify by pulling out the largest square factor: \(\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}\). Add only like surds: \(2\sqrt{3} + 5\sqrt{3} = 7\sqrt{3}\).

Rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by the surd, or by the conjugate \(a - \sqrt{b}\) for a two-term denominator.

Bounds lie half a unit each side of a rounded value. To make \(\frac{a}{b}\) largest, use the upper bound of a and the lower bound of b.

steps: Rationalise \(\frac{1}{a + \sqrt{b}}\): multiply top and bottom by the conjugate \(a - \sqrt{b}\). The denominator becomes \(a^2 - b\), a whole number.
Square a surd: \((a + \sqrt{b})^2 = a^2 + 2a\sqrt{b} + b\). Keep the middle term.
Bound of \(\frac{a}{b}\): the largest value uses upper \(a\) and lower \(b\); the smallest uses lower \(a\) and upper \(b\).
gold.title: Gold: conjugates, surd squares and bounds of a quotient

steps: Simplify a surd: find the largest square number that divides it, then take its root outside. \(\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25 \times 2} = 5\sqrt{2}\).
Add or subtract only surds with the same root: add the numbers in front, keep the root. \(2\sqrt{3} + 5\sqrt{3} = 7\sqrt{3}\).
Bounds: half a unit each side of the rounded value. To the nearest cm the half unit is 0.5; to 1 d.p. it is 0.05.
bronze.title: Bronze: one surd or one bound

steps: Multiply or divide: combine under one root, then simplify. \(\sqrt{8} \times \sqrt{6} = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\).
Rationalise \(\frac{n}{\sqrt{a}}\): multiply top and bottom by \(\sqrt{a}\), then simplify the fraction.
Bounds of a sum: for the smallest \(a + b\), add both lower bounds; for the largest, add both upper bounds.
